utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Could the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. This is case number IT-05-88/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. As this is the first day of our hearings of evidence, I would kindly ask for appearances now. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Peter McCloskey, and with me is Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God bless you and peace to this house. My name is Zdravko Tolimir and my legal counsel is Aleksandar Gajic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before the first witness is being brought in, the Chamber would like to raise the following matters. The Chamber is seized of the accused's request to the Trial Chamber concerning the role of the accused's legal advisor, Mr. Gajic, filed in English on the 3rd of March, 2010, and has in the meantime received a response of the Prosecution and the reply from the accused. The Chamber has also received a Rule 33(B) submission from OLAD which was filed only this morning. Firstly, the Chamber notes that you, Mr. Tolimir, have made this submission at a very late stage of these proceedings. Taking into consideration the postponed commencement of this trial, this matter should have been brought to the Chamber's attention much earlier. However, as it is a very serious matter and as the Chamber has only recently received all relevant submissions, it will need to consider the accused's requests carefully and will render a written decision as soon as possible. Secondly, the Chamber would like to issue an oral decision concerning protective measures for the witness number 40. This decision relates to the Prosecution's confidential motion filed before the Chamber on the 8th of March, 2010, concerning the continuation of protective measures for Witness 40. The Chamber reiterates that Rule 75(F)(i) provides that: "Once protective measures have been ordered in respect of a victim or witness in any proceedings before the Tribunal ... such protective measures ... shall continue to have effect mutatis mutandis in any other proceeding before the Tribunal ... unless and until they are rescinded, varied, or augmented in accordance with the procedure set out in Rule 75." The Chamber notes that the Rules do not impose any obligation on a party wishing to present the testimony of a witness subject to protective measures to provide justification for their continuation. Also, if such a party were to be obliged to justify the continuation of the protective measures, Rule 75(F)(i) would in effect be nullified. If, however, a party were to seek to rescind, vary, or augment protective measures ordered in respect of a witness in any proceedings before the Tribunal, Rule 75(G)(i) requires this party to apply to the Chamber that initially ordered the protective measures in case it remains seized of the proceedings in which such an order was issued. The Chamber notes that the Trial Chamber in Popovic et al. remains seized of the proceedings in which it ordered the protective measures for Witness 40, and therefore is competent to rescind, vary, or augment those protective measures. The present Chamber would therefore not be competent to vary, augment, or rescind protective measures concerning Witness 40. Since the protective measures ordered for Witness 40 in the Popovic et al. case have not been rescinded, varied, or augmented in accordance with the procedure set out in Rule 75, these protective measures continue to have effect in the instant case. The motion of the Prosecution is accordingly granted. Furthermore, the Chamber would like to inform the parties that we will not sit in the week after Easter, in order to enable everybody to celebrate these holidays appropriately. The last hearing before will be on the 30th of March and the first after Easter on the 14th of April. And, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber is still seized of your request to change the hearing time for the 29th of March. We hope to find a way to reschedule the hearing of that day. Finally, I would like to inform the parties that we have a limited sitting time tomorrow evening. Due to another commitment, we will have to adjourn shortly after 6.00 p.m. tomorrow, and please keep in mind that we will usually, and today, have two breaks, the first at 3.45 and the second at 5.30 if that seems to be convenient for everybody. If the parties would prefer different sitting times and break times, then the Chamber will consider this. Could the witness please now be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, first I would like to tell you the Chamber has granted protective measures. You should be aware of that. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I will be referring to you as "witness," as you know is the practice here. But the first thing I want to do is show you this sheet of paper, which is 65 ter 6118. And can you tell us if that is your name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll get our practice down. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session for the first few questions. I think that would keep the protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us where you settled around Srebrenica. We know it's a big -- it was a big area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in Srebrenica, there was a Bosniak there, and in Kazani near the graveyard, he was waiting there, and he offered accommodation. He made an arrangement with my older brother and we stayed with this man in his house until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know that Srebrenica is a town in a narrow valley. Was this in the town itself or was it in one of the little villages or rural areas outside the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we lived in the town near the hospital, near the two high-rise buildings. Anyone who knows Srebrenica knows what I'm talking about. It was closer to the UNPROFOR base, and that is town proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me take you to July 1995 and ask you: Were you living in this same place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you in the BiH army, the Muslim army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do to sustain yourself, to feed yourself and your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were sowing land, that was Serbian land that had been abandoned, and we were working the land. That's how we sustained ourselves, in addition to receiving some of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at some point in July 1995, did you decide to leave your home once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had to. That wasn't our decision of our own accord. We just had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the Serbian forces were pushing to take and capture Srebrenica at any cost, and that is the reason why we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you continue to want to live in Srebrenica if it had become controlled by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody remained in Srebrenica. Nobody dared remain except handicapped people, which they, the Serbian forces, probably killed if they came across such handicapped people. Everybody else had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said "nobody dared." What were people afraid of -- and yourself I'm mostly concerned about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid of what actually happened to us. We were afraid of dying, and this is exactly what happened to us later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what course of action you took and when. You remember the dates well, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, that was a Tuesday, we decided to leave. Those fit for military service decided to go through the woods, while the elder men, women, and children decided to go to Potocari, and they also took to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to this had there been any military action or -- in and around the town of Srebrenica where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard from other people that there was some action outside of town, but not in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was there any shelling that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. On that day, the 11th of July, I saw the footage that was played here in the courtroom. I saw women entering the UNPROFOR compound. They were around some trucks, and you can see that there was a shell that had landed approximately 100 metres from the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's important, Witness, to distinguish between what you actually saw at the time and what you may have seen in video later. The Court will be able to see these videos, and so what we want from you now is what you remember seeing and happening to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment when the shell landed, there was a crowd of people headed for Potocari. There was no transportation provided for them, and the distance was about 4 kilometres. When this mortar landed above the UNPROFOR base, all the women and children tried to find shelter in the UNPROFOR base and their trucks. I saw it with my own eyes, but that was the time when I was leaving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And who did you leave Srebrenica with on this day, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my brother Nurif.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Susnjari, through woods and meadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everybody decided to take that route, not to Tuzla but rather to Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any idea of roughly how many people gathered around the area of Susnjari on these -- on this day, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to some rough estimates, there should have been at least 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you get this rough estimate from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what we did discuss amongst ourselves. We just tried to reach a certain figure because if you think that a football stadium can accommodate 15.000 people, that was the kind of bench-mark for us to make this estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many of those people were armed with rifles or some gun of some sort roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 200 and 500 rifles they had, but only rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened up there on the 11th, what did you do? What did the rest of the group do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in the evening of the 11th to Susnjari. Some left immediately during the night, and I myself left Susnjari the next day, that is, the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And left going where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother who never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you with a lot of other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a column, an endless column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly where you were in this endless column, beginning, middle, end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the rear end of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you just briefly describe to us what you did on that 12th when you set off with the column through the woods towards Tuzla, with your brother and this other group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We walked until darkness. That was a thick forest, and I spent the night under a beech tree because I didn't sleep the previous night because there was panic everywhere. So I slept the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know the area at all, what features or other areas, anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I was in that area for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us an idea of how hot was it on this -- these July days and nights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at night. It was hot during the night -- during the day, but not at night. Nights were rather chilly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on your walk on the 12th, were you fired upon by any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were firing on us, but I didn't feel the bullets passing next to us; they were falling astray, somewhere behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when you woke up on the morning of the 13th, can you tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I woke up that morning, I saw some people coming back and some were going forward, and I went a little bit back with this group that was retreating. After that, I again saw a group moving forward. But my brother wasn't there any longer. I returned again to the group that was going forward and I saw many more people there, including my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sitting there and the Serb started calling upon us through the megaphone to surrender. Since we ourselves didn't have a megaphone, we had to shout very loudly, "Yes, we shall do that but to the UNPROFOR and the Red Cross." They didn't respond anything to that. They only gave us an ultimatum, which was to expire at 10.00 and at which time they said they would attack us. After 10.00 they again started calling us. People again asked for UNPROFOR and the Red Cross, and they gave us a new dead-line which was 1500 hours. Then people started discussing whether to surrender or not. We thought there was no way out of that situation, and it was decided for us to surrender. I saw people carrying a white T-shirt attached to a staff as a sign of surrender. Then we went through a wood, and when we came to a field we saw a lot of dead bodies. That was probably where an ambush had been set for this first group, and we didn't know anything about this because we were at the rear end of the column. While we were descended, it was a very steep slope and we went down to a river. First we had a lot of water to drink. When we came down there, there were Serbian soldiers awaiting us. These Serbian soldiers immediately asked us to give them money. They were asking us to give them US dollars, German marks, and any currency, and they said, "If you don't give it to us, those who were your predecessors were -- actually, you will fare in the same way as your predecessors," but I don't know who those predecessors were. Once we reached the road, we had our hands up in the air. They lined us along the road, and that is when women and children arrived in buses. There was not a single adult male among them. There was my wife's aunt and another woman that I knew from before. We were told to take out everything from our pockets. At the time I was smoking tobacco and I threw that tobacco and the lighter on the road. Another soldier told us, "You better take this, you might need it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You said the decision was made for you to surrender. Do you know who made that decision for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We ourselves amongst us decided it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any military people among the group you were in, any Bosnian Muslim military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Those who had some weapons, they had left with the first group and they had moved through. And they were lucky because they had the weapons, whereas we didn't have anything and we could be killed by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This road where you went down and surrendered, was this a -- what was this road made out of? What kind of road was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as we kept going down the slope, we went through the woods, and then we crossed one or two fields, and then we reached a paved road, the main road that led from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is this -- where was the area that you saw the women and children being transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was at the place where we surrendered, around Sandici approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that at the asphalt road at Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on that asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know just roughly what time of day it was that you got down to the Sandici area on the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was perhaps 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did people in your group have back-packs, any personal belongings with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had them. I had a back-pack myself, and we when we -- as we were getting ready to step on to the asphalt road they said, "Why don't you just throw your back-packs there, by the side of the road, and they will follow you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear for our record, when you say "they," who was the one who told you to throw your stuff by the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what happened in the afternoon there at Sandici with this -- your group that had surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we surrendered, we actually reached an elevation some hundred metres away from the road, and there were rows and rows of people - I don't know how many. There was an APC there and a Serb soldier, a very young soldier, who had a black kerchief around his head. I don't know what that was supposed to mean, but he was in charge. Whenever a group arrived or ran across, then he would tell the group, "Tomorrow you will be exchanged, all for all." And as we were sitting in rows, there was a soldier by every single row, one on the one side and another on the other side. There were -- in our row there were two women and a young woman and a young boy, he was that woman's son. And the soldier with a black kerchief said to the woman, "There are buses down there." Then the young girl and the other young girl, who was very pretty, got up and the Serb soldier started saying, "No, no, leave them behind, we need her." Well, this guy wasn't really paying any attention to them. He said, "Just go to the bus." And he let go probably some 10 or so more boys, who were up to 15 years of age. And then there was another boy, I don't know how old he was, I didn't dare turn around. He said, "No, no, you remain seated. You are able to carry a machine-gun."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any more military equipment beside this APC, armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, it's just that they were armed, they had rifles. And when another group was supposed to come over as a new shift, they started saying, "Well, here are Arkan's men." I couldn't really tell what kind of insignia they had on their uniforms. I just noticed that they had new uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you see any buses or trucks moving along the road with women and children in them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see the road from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened then after you were placed in this meadow with this big group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while we were there, on that meadow, they ordered us to lie down on our stomachs. We all did. And they told us we should keep calling "Allahu Akbar," which is a Muslim prayer. Then they began to yell at us, saying, "This is not Srebrenica." And then they told us to start calling out, "Long live the king." Well, people started doing that, I don't know if I did myself, but in any case they couldn't tell who was actually calling out and who wasn't. And I -- all this time I had this thought in the back of my mind that they weren't going to shoot us in that position. But we know that there were instances where - and that's what happened in Zvornik and that's how my brother-in-law was killed - they just ordered people to lie down on their stomachs, and then -- women and men and children, and then they just shot them in the back. And that's -- I know about this because I was told by my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't want to ask you about Zvornik and what happened in 1992 or what was told to you, but what did you think was going to happen to you when you were all told to lie down on your stomachs and say these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I thought that they weren't going to shoot us because there was a soldier -- well, there would have to be a soldier coming along the rows from one side and another from the other end on the other side if they were going to shoot us, but they didn't do that so I thought they wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this, people started yelling, "Here's Mladic, here's Mladic coming." Up until then I hadn't seen Mladic ever. I was in Srebrenica. I didn't watch TV and I didn't know the man from before or what he looked like, but he came along, he came with a few soldiers with him, and he called out to us and said, "Good evening, neighbours." And he said, "Tomorrow you will be exchanged, everyone will be exchanged, all for all." And we said, "Thank you, commander." And we started clapping our hands. Then he left, and soon afterwards they ordered us -- they ordered the first row, the first line of people, to climb on to the vehicle and then the second row, third, and so on, up until it came my turn. And then as I came on to the road they started yelling, "You have to get on to this truck." And it so happened that I ended up being in the trailer of the truck. And then I saw a young soldier, maybe up -- not older than 30. He had a short beard and a black bandanna, and he said, "I will go with this -- on this truck and go with the soldier." He didn't address us. So as soon as the vehicle would be filled with people, it would leave. Soon night fell and we had no idea where we were going. Vehicles passed us by. We could just see the lights, the headlights of vehicles passing us by. We headed towards Bratunac, and when we arrived there, on the left-hand side one could see buildings up to three to four storeys high, but on the right-hand side we couldn't see any buildings. The vehicle -- they parked the vehicle at the end of the street or on the side of the street actually. And one of them, the driver, who was a driver and who was with us in the trailer, said, "These are Vihor garages." Soon after that they began asking for people from the Srebrenica villages to come out, Pusmulici, Glogova, Slatina, Konjevic Polje, and so on, a number of other villages, I don't know anymore which, and as soon as these people would step forward they would ask for their father's name and then take them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you briefly. You said "they asked," who were these "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you said there's a truck with a trailer. Can you give us an idea how big this truck and trailer was so we can get a picture. Is it a big construction or a small little personal truck and trailer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, these were trucks. These were big construction trucks that would transport iron ore or coal and so on. They were big, maybe 12 or 13 metres long. They're big trucks. But the trailer was also very big, it was at least 10 metres long. So if you're sitting on the truck, you wouldn't see a person sitting in the cab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you see over the top of the trailer where you were held or -- if you stood up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know where we were headed. That's why I was saying we just noticed -- and again, the brother of mine who came back, he said that he had seen people between Bratunac and Glogova. He was on the bus, and he was the one who told me, "Well, here they just drove away captured people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just clear something up. You said someone came back and told you this. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, my brother said, once I reached the free territory, that he had seen when those buses and trucks drove off towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's why I needed to clarify that. Let's just try to stay right in Bratunac at the moment. But can you tell us how high the sides of this trailer were in -- that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were perhaps 1 metre high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did -- were you able to stand up and look over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't dare stand up. No one dared even place their arm over this side of the truck. If they did that, they would be just hit with the rifle-butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then tell us what happened as -- you've said that the Serb soldiers were calling people out from Srebrenica villages. Did anybody respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, people responded, and then they would take that person upward, they would take them away; and then we would hear a strong thud. And then you could hear cries. They would start yelling, "Stop that, stop that," then you would hear a gun-shot, and then there would be silence. And that's how it went on that whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did any of the people that left during the night like this come back, any of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened in the morning? And this would be now the morning of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the morning when it grew lighter, the Serb soldiers started yelling, "Don't allow civilians to go up to that street." They were probably afraid that one of the civilians would then report what they had seen there and what had happened. They told us then, "Now, take them to Fikret and Alija and exchange them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I stop you here. We don't receive interpretation at the moment. Try it again. Is there interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's start over. There was a little interpretation glitch. So can you tell us, that morning, after these comments about Alija, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, they said that these people should now be taken to Fikret and Alija and exchanged. The trucks and buses set off, and then as they reached the edge of Bratunac they were stopped again. And then they said, "We're waiting for UNPROFOR." It got really hot there because the sides of the truck were metal, the sun was shining. And the driver who drove us and another young man from Bratunac brought water for us, they gave us water, but we were so thirsty that we never had enough. They kept bringing water, but it wasn't enough to slake our thirst. The young man who was from Bratunac started asking about a man Ismet, last name Ramic, who was a shoemaker, started asking about him. And then somebody asked him, "Well, why are you asking about him?" And he said, "Well, he was my neighbour."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did this group of vehicles stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth I didn't have a watch, but it took a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly what time in the morning it -- the trucks first started moving before it stopped at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was very early. It could have been 6.00 or 6.30 in the morning. It was very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then it stops for a while and then what happens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this, when neither UNPROFOR appeared nor anyone, there was a group of civilians, Serb civilians, who appeared, elderly people. Some of them were in uniforms, others weren't, and they were on a truck. It was an old Srebrenica truck that people used to transport humanitarian aid. And this group, they said, "They're coming behind us." What they meant by that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: These are ours. What they meant by that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then a column started. We stopped just once for maybe five minutes, and then the column moved forward towards Konjevic Polje. And as we were walking [as interpreted] towards Konjevic Polje and climbing up the hill, it was only then that we could actually see. I don't know whether there were five trucks or ten trucks, but as we were driving and we were up on the hill, then we could see the entire column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what could you see when you saw this entire column, can you give us an idea of the size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could see that there were three armoured vehicles in one place. I don't know whether they were waiting for somebody or not, but they were there, and it was then that we set out towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the English a while back, it said that you were walking up the hill. Were you ever walking at this point or that may have just been a translation mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were driving. We were driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you -- where did this column of vehicles go towards from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where is the next place it stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we came to Josanica, one could see Divic from there, and some people started yelling that there was an APC of the UN in front of the Vidikovac hotel that joined us. We passed through Divic -- it wasn't called Divic at the time, it was called St. Stephen, Sveti Stefan. It was quite steep, and when I looked back I could see that the sign read "Sveti Stefan."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this place a little village just south of Zvornik, right on the cliffs above the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's right by the Drina River, right next to it. It's -- it has about 3 to 4.000 inhabitants. It's quite densely populated. Houses are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what colour was this APC that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was white.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did your vehicles go from Divic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved back to Zvornik, and from there to Karakaj. And then from Karakaj, the trucks turned left towards Tuzla. We drove for a short period of time, and then the trucks turned to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when they turned to the -- was the -- the road when you went towards Tuzla, was that a small road or a main road, the one going towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the main road from Zvornik to Tuzla, and the one that we were on was a minor road, regional road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before you turned off on this minor road, where did you think you were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when they started towards Tuzla -- and prior to that they kept promising that we would be exchanged. And at that point in time I truly thought that they were going to exchange us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you returned right onto this minor road, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to this village called Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the elementary school in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened when your vehicle got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came in front of the yard, the vehicles would enter one by one or perhaps two or three at the same time into the yard. They would unload the prisoners, and prisoners would need to run into the school building. When our turn came, we entered the -- the yard and the UN APC did not have the UN sign anymore. It just had a C remaining there. And there were two soldiers with automatic weapons, and then there was a civilian there, between 50 and 55 years of age, moving about. None of them said anything to anyone. There were Serbian soldiers there. Now, whether they captured the UN APC, I don't know. When we got off the truck, we were ordered to run into the school building. When I was just in front of the door, I had a leather jacket on me and they told me to take the jacket off. And I took it off and I put it on a pile of other clothing, and I entered through the hallway. We went straight for a while and then we turned left. It was a long hallway that took us to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when someone told you to take off your coat, was that a civilian or a military person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military person. Civilians did not interfere into anything there. There were civilians just standing and watching but not saying anything to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to get any idea of how many soldiers were standing around as you got hustled off the bus and moved into the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, both the police and the soldiers, there were perhaps up to 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you distinguish police from soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, policemen had grey-olive uniforms and soldiers had green multi-coloured uniforms. Later on when the corridor was opened, I saw what uniform policemen had because we only had one police where we lived, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when a military man told you to take off your jacket and put it in that -- that pile, can you give us some idea about how big a pile of belongings were of other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a large pile, perhaps hundred to 200 people had taken their clothes off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you describe what the gym was like when you got in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered the gym, it was more than half full, and as people entered they would sit down. And we would sit down in such a way as to have our knees touch our chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, you know, we say "gym," but can you describe what sort of facility this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, in elementary schools there's a sports hall where kids have physical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there basketball backboards there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened when you got in and had to sit like you described? Tell us what else happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when everybody entered the gym, they put a blanket down and four young boys sat there. They were between 10 and 14 years of age, I would say. When I crossed into the free territory I immediately asked whether four kids had been released, and I was told that yes. That means that if they hadn't released those four kids they would have killed people from 10 to 80 years of age because people who were there had been brought in from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened after you saw these kids were on the -- they were allowed to sit on a blanket. What happened to everybody else as you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would pick out prisoners to bring water for us, and they would bring water. And then after a long period of time a delegation of officers or some other persons like that came, and one of them asked whether there was anybody there from the Zvornik municipality and nobody responded. Then they ordered that four rows should get up. Those were the elderly from Potocari. And they told them to turn around, face the wall, and have their backs towards the door. Then they called another four rows and then another four rows. And when my turn came, when four of my rows got up, we faced in the other direction and our backs were turned towards the exit where there was Serbian soldiers and a woman. And then they brought a lot of cloth, and it went on until one of us prisoners said, "You must not kill these people." It was mostly young men standing at the door, 18 or younger, Serbian soldiers, and they all held their rifles in their hands like that. And the one that uttered those words, he was maybe 25. And then they said, "Well, who says so?" And the man again repeated the same words. And then they said, "Well, we'll see whether we must or we must not," and then they told them to get up. He had black trousers on him and a shirt similar to mine. They took him out of the gym. We heard rifle shots and the man screamed, and then more shots and then silence. Then they took out a young man again, 20 to 25. I don't know why they took him out. Again we heard rifle shots and the man never re-appeared. They stopped the water from being brought in. I guess they needed time to clear that away, and then they started putting blindfolds on us. And we would go into this room that was L-shaped. Before that people asked them, "Where are you taking these people?" And they responded, "To Bijeljina, to a camp there." Nobody put any questions after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you for just one minute. In one of your statements within a year or so after the events, it appears from that -- in the statement that the people that were -- got up that said, "Don't kill any of us," that they were killed in the gym in front of you. Is that correct, or is your recollection now that they were actually taken outside and that's when you heard shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I never said that he was killed in the gym. He was taken out, and the other one was taken out as well. Right there, I only saw them slap one man. Why they slapped him, I don't know. People addressed the soldiers. They would say, "Soldiers." And they would respond saying, "We are not soldiers. We are Karadzic's Chetniks." So nobody was killed there. People were taken out in front of the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in this gym, how full was it with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had to sit with our knees against our chests, and there were between 500 and 1.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was there any empty space in this gym or was it pretty full up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, when all of us were there in the gym, you couldn't throw a matchstick and have it fall on the floor, and that was before people started going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how hot was it in that gym that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was so hot that people started complaining. You could just hear a rumour, and then Serbian soldiers would fire on the wall to make them go quiet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was some elderly men from Potocari. So when you say "elderly," how old did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a man from my village, I knew him, he was 70. And these people were between 60- and 70-something. I know that this one man from my village was 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say from Potocari, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the people who had left with women and children as not fit for the army service, it was them, not just those who went to Orahovac. Everywhere, at every location, young and old alike were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you know that these men were from the group that went with the women and children to Potocari? Did you know that at the time or is that something you learned later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We knew immediately that those people had gone with women and children because they were so frail that they couldn't walk 5 kilometres in the whole day, let alone 100 kilometres from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you give us any kind of a rough time estimate of when you actually first got to this school. When your truck first pulled up to the school, do you know roughly what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. It was in the afternoon. But I didn't have a watch on me, so I don't know what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you jammed in this gym until you were stood up and blindfolded and put in this L-shaped room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how long we spent there, but when I came out there was maybe one hour before it fell dark. I don't know whether we were there for three hours, five hours. I haven't got a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us what happened in the L-shaped room and -- where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they took two prisoners there and blindfolded them. There was a woman standing there and two uniformed men. The woman also wore uniform. She gave a cup of water to every person after they had been blindfolded. Why she did that, I don't know. They made a kind of swing barrier there and there was a TAM truck there. When I boarded the truck there were two benches but they were not full. I sat on the right-hand side. When the truck became full and all the places on the benches were occupied, people were sitting down between the benches. I forgot to say that once they started taking people out, a soldier appeared with a red beret. He went with every batch of people. I don't know whether there were two or three trucks, because once you have a blindfold you can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just tell us briefly what a TAM truck is so we can get that picture of a TAM truck in our mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TAM truck was used by farmers to transport produce and cattle. It is good for small cattle. It could perhaps accommodate two cows but not more, so mostly people from Bijeljina and Janja used these kind of trucks for the transportation of agriculture produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did the military use TAM trucks as well with benches on the side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The army never had this kind of trucks. They had bigger TAM trucks, but they confiscated these smaller ones from the farmers because they commandeered all kind of machinery from farmers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this door that you went out and were -- from a ramp into the truck, was this the same door you came in to the building or a different one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we entered through a different door and we went out through this door. In 1999 I went to visit the scene, and that is when this door was -- was built and closed with concrete blocks because terrible genocide was carried out in the territory of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did you go there with in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went with this investigator named Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was an investigator from the ICTY, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he took you to this school, were you able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, once you were put in the back of this truck with your blindfold, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck rode down an asphalt road for a short period of time. I felt that it went to the left. After this short ride it stopped. We were told to climb down, and that's what we did. I looked in front of myself and I saw a dead man. I have three children and immediately I thought about them, and I thought that I would have the same destiny like this man, that I'm not going to see my children ever again. And I was -- I started praying to God and I started thinking in what way they are going to kill me. A burst of fire was heard coming from the left. I fell down and my right arm was across the chest of another man. When this burst of fire stopped, a man came, started walking among the people lying on the ground and shooting them in the head. I have a little bruise here probably from the ground and the gravel that was on the road --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just interrupt you for the record. I see you're pointing to some fingers on your right hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've told us you had a blindfold on. How can you see anything with this blindfold, was it still on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see this on my hand. I only felt it. But at that very moment, because I was looking down in front of myself, I saw this dead man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you have the blindfold on when you looked down to see the dead man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was just looking directly in front of me, because you couldn't see anything ahead. That was a very sick -- thick cloth and it wasn't see-through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after the firing and you fell down, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When everything stopped, when the shooting stopped, they started shouting, "Let's go and take their watches off." I didn't have a watch and my left arm was beneath me, but then one of them said, "We're not going to do that," and they didn't. In the meantime, as soon as a truck would arrive the same would be repeated. You would hear a burst of fire and all this was going on until darkness fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us -- and -- just your rough estimate of how long this -- these executions were going on from the time you first got to this site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it -- they definitely lasted until 11.00 in the evening because it lasted for quite some time after darkness fell. Overall I don't know how long it started from the very -- how long it took from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any lights around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an excavator there, and it was digging. When I slowly removed my blindfold I saw this excavator opposite us. When this was finished, they didn't have any more place and they all gathered around this machine, and this man who was in charge told them, "Let's go to this field where grass had been cut to kill all those people." The man stopped the excavator and said, "If you leave, I'd like to go with you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any names mentioned by any of these men that were doing the shooting or were at the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They mentioned the names Gojko, Vojo, that's how they were addressing one another, Risto. This Gojko was my fellow worker from the company and we had known each other for 15 years. Gojko thought that all the men were dead, and he said that he would like to be kissed by some of the men who were killed. I recognised his voice when he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see his face while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. It was dark. It was night-time. I couldn't see his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how can you be sure it was this voice of this Gojko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had a very specific voice. If you know someone for a long time you can recognise their voice everywhere, and as I said, we knew each other for 15 years. And they also were addressing one another by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's a good time to take a break, and I can also tell you we're getting close to being finished with direct examination. Maybe another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we break, my fellow Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question. Witness PW-007, I would like to know exactly what happened on July 12th. In the transcript, page 15, line 8, 9, and 10, it says the following, and I'll read in English: [In English] "No, no. Those who had some weapons, they had left with the first group and they had moved through, and they were lucky because they had their weapons, whereas we didn't have anything and we could be killed by anyone." [Interpretation] This is on page 15. But on page 14, line 12, this is what I read: [In English] "We went through a wood and when we came to a field, we saw a lot of dead bodies. That was probably where an ambush had been set for this first group, and we didn't know anything about this because we were at the rear end of the column." [Interpretation] So this is my question, Witness. If I understand things correctly, the first group had weapons, so these dead bodies were probably people who had been killed during a battle. I don't know. It's just a question. I don't know what happened. So why are you saying later on that the first group was lucky because they had weapons, if they were killed at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not all of them were killed. Probably 50 people were killed, but these people were killed on their way from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about this first group where there were people with weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not all of them were armed. Those who had weapons advanced and went ahead. Among them were, for example, the president of the municipality, the people who had to be provided with some security, and nobody knew what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this kind of genocide never happened anywhere after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I could have one follow-up question that may help clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of how many -- roughly how many men from the beginning of the Muslim column actually made it through at Baljkovica and made it through to Muslim lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them. Maybe you should ask someone else. I never asked about this and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are those the lucky ones that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. Anyone who managed to cross over could be considered lucky. Those who were unlucky are now being exhumed from various graves, one arm in one grave, one leg in another grave. So only those who survived were lucky. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was again no translation of the last part. There might be a problem with the system in the moment, but I think you could deal with this problem after the break, again to clarify the situation. We must have our first break now and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00. And I think to enable the witness to leave the courtroom we should go into private -- it's not necessary. You will deal with that. Thank you very much. The Court Officer will assist you during the break. We will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if the booth caught that last sentence and they can tell us or not. I can try to see if the witness remembers what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the interpreters didn't get this last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll try to slow it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, you had -- in answering my last question had said that the lucky ones were the ones that made it through and that the unlucky ones were the ones that were in mass graves. And then you said something else which the interpreters -- we weren't able to get. Do you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said only those who were in mass graves had their limbs in different graves and maybe of -- it was necessary to dig in to three or four graves in order to put together one person and his body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So have you been following the exhumations of these mass graves by the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only heard that the majority of these graves were dug out. They did find my brother, but not his complete body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else, if anything, did you hear Gojko say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said, "Collect all your ammunition, let's go to this mowed field and let's shoot the people." He seemed, he appeared, to be the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you when you heard him say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some 10 to 20 metres from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned an excavator. Can you describe to the Court what you mean by excavator, what kind of excavator -- or not the brand name, but there's lots of big digging equipment. Can you tell us what it is you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is a construction machine used for digging trenches and canals. It can also load cargo on but it has a small bucket, so it's different. It's really a digger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you see another kind of a machine there besides this excavator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after this I saw a loader. This loader came with the lights on because the excavator was turned in the opposite direction so the lights were only used -- the excavator lights were only used to actually throw some light on the area that is being excavated or dug up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what happened after this, after you saw this digging equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when the digger, or rather, the loader arrived, it had the lights on and we were all lit up. One of us was alive and he was on the other side, on the opposite side from where we were. So he sort of stood up and ran into the woods. They fired after him, and the driver of this digger turned the digger so that he could actually light up the area where the man fled into the woods. And at that moment I moved and then he said, "Well, there's another man moving here." Fortunately, they didn't hear him, and then I just lay -- I just took two long strides and I could feel some stones there. And then I looked around. When I saw that no one was going in my direction, I stood up. And as I ran up this embankment, a stone-built embankment, I realised that it was really rail tracks there. I ran up and I could hear a burst of fire being fired behind me. I didn't see or hear the bullets actually hit the stones around me and I didn't feel being hit. I flew over the railway tracks, and then I just threw myself over the other side of the embankment. I jumped up again on to my feet, and then I realised that there was a maise field not far off. They were already very tall, the corn stalks. I ran halfway, and then I thought they will start shooting because they will see the corn rustling. And then I just threw myself on the ground, and then as I slithered through it, I realised that there was some stream or water somewhere, but I didn't see it. The Serb soldiers went searching through the cornfield. They shot just randomly, I don't think -- and I didn't feel that anything hit me. And then they turned back and went away. I could hear the shooting for a long time after that, and when everything was over, I got myself up from the cornfield. There was a copse of trees not far from there, but I was very afraid as I left the cornfield into the open field, but there was no one there, fortunately, because had there been someone they would have caught me and killed me, I am sure. And then I started moving but I didn't really know where I was going because I knew when they had brought us to the school, but from there onwards, I didn't know where I was. And then as I was walking along the paved road there was -- there were bodies there, but there were signs of life from one of these persons. He was -- the sound that he was producing was inhuman. It was almost like an animal squealing, but I couldn't really help him. So I moved along and then I came across the railway tracks again, and then as I crossed them I realised that I was at the railway station in Orahovac. So I concluded that I was again heading in the direction of Zvornik. So I re-traced my steps. I went back and got on to the road again. I didn't know where I was going. I decided to go into the wood because I was afraid it would get light, because it was a summer night and they're not very long. I headed from there towards a home. There was a light coming from there. I didn't hear any sound, not even a dog barking, and then as I passed by a hut, I saw a person sleeping there with a rifle against the wall. And then I went around that house, and again I had no idea where I was. Soon after that it grew light. I went through some villages that had been burnt down. I know they were Bosniak villages because they had been burnt down. I had no idea where I was going. The sun was high up and I still had no idea where I was going. But as I walked on, fortunately I was walking in the right direction, not in the opposite direction, and once I reached Krizevici where a store used to be, I knew -- I found my bearings, I knew where I was. So then I retraced my steps a bit. I went backwards. And then as I went up a slope, I saw that a mosque which used to be there had been destroyed. And then I arrived in Seferovici. I knew that because I had some relatives nearby, in a village nearby, and as I was there, there was a patrol that was walking there and they started shooting, but I managed to get through Seferovici, this village. I walked across some grass. The houses were all burnt down. And then as I crossed over that field, I realised that there was this village that I knew, that I was familiar with, because I had some relatives there. The grass was so high that I was wet almost up to my waist. So then I decided to take a nap. I lay down and slept for maybe an hour or two, I have no idea how long, but when I woke up I realised I hadn't eaten anything for a very long time because we were only given water, nothing else, since we had been detained. Maybe I had a fruit or something but -- so then I went down to the village and I found a pear which was ripe. There were some green buds or fruits on fruit trees, but I couldn't eat that. There was only this one pear. So then I tried to find some clothes in the village -there was no one there because it had been burnt down - because I wanted a change of clothes because the shirt that I had on had a blood-stain because of the man who had leaned against me who had been shot. So I wanted to make sure that I had clean clothes because had they found me like that, they would have known that I had escaped. So I returned -- I started going back. I headed back toward Baljkovica when it got dark and I found a house that remained almost intact. It hadn't been completely burnt down. The roof was -- had fallen in, but -- but the walls were still up. And then when I arrived there there were three buses, Drinatrans buses that were going -- local buses that were transporting people back from -- towards Baljkovici. The direction the buses were going was a Serb village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then I decided to spend the night in that house. And in the morning, when it got light, somebody threw something, flung a stone against the wall and said, "Get up." So I got up and I just was expecting someone to barge the door --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one second. I'm sorry, you had mentioned a village just now but they weren't able to hear it. Can you tell us what village you had just passed through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was Delici, that was the name of the village. I know -- I was not from that village, but I know -- I have a general idea, and I think it's Delici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Delici or Dulici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And now from this morning that someone threw a rock at you, how many more days did it take you to reach the Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, had the road been clear it would have taken 15 to 20 minutes because I was already nearby, but the roads weren't clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how long did it take you to manage to get away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I actually took advantage of the situation then because the people who were going from Srebrenica had arrived at Baljkovica at that time, and had there not been a breakthrough at that time of the front line, those people would have ended the same way we had. And then when they arrived there, the Serbs had withdrawn all their artillery from Baljkovica. So I took advantage of that situation and sort of flew over to the other side. I was so close. There were some hundred metres or so where I could see the houses on the other side, but it was all a clearing and I was afraid that someone might notice me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say the people from Srebrenica made a breakthrough through Baljkovica, are those people from Srebrenica, is that part of the column that you were speaking of earlier, the front of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there -- was that where the weapons were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most probably. I don't know. I wasn't with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And -- okay. Now let me take you back briefly to something you mentioned. You said you didn't get any food during this time, but let me ask you when you were at Sandici, the area next to this asphalt road where you surrendered, did you see the Serb forces providing anyone with any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were people there, wounded people. They were crying out, asking for them to be -- for their wounds to be dressed, but then they moved and went on to another house and they never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who were moved on to another house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the wounded people were taken to a house there. There were some houses there some 200 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any of the Muslims that were in that field with you near Sandici get treated with any kind of first aid or medical or receive any help of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They just offered a bottle of liquor and they offered a few people to have a swig and maybe a cigarette or two, but there was no food or any medical assistance provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there some water provided at Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did bring water for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in that truck that you were in from the time you left Sandici, you spent the night in that truck in Bratunac, and you were taken to that truck the next morning to Orahovac, did anyone bring you any food or anybody else in that truck bring you any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For the entire period since we had been captured, no one had seen a crumb of food. They did give us water, not that evening but on the next day, both in Bratunac and in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, once you got to the school in Orahovac, before you were put in an execution line, did anyone give anybody any food in that gym or any medical attention of any sort that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody. They just put a bucket for people to relieve themselves and there was nothing else. They did bring water, but there wasn't enough for everybody to fill themselves up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back briefly again to Sandici, did you see any of the soldiers or police taking down names and making lists of the Muslim men or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They did not write down any of the prisoners. I don't know about what happened in other locations. This is why the Serbs are claiming that it wasn't that number of people who got killed. They don't know exactly whom they killed and how many. They could have killed people of any ethnicity. They asked whether there were any Serbs among us, but there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm just going to show you some photos that I know you've seen many times before in your previous testimonies, but let's put them on your screen, so you should, I think, get your glasses out. The first one is number 1129, 65 ter 1129. It should appear on your screen and we're going to try to use that writing pencil that you used before, but I want you to just take a look at this photograph to see if it means anything to you. And while we're waiting, do you remember how many times you've come to The Hague to testify in the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my fifth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wonder if this can be blown up a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, just take a look at that. It's obviously winter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went out through this area here. This is where the ramp was where we got on to the TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hold on, it disappeared. This is our first photo of the trial, so bear with us for a second. Could you just, to make it simple put a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Officer will help you. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you take that pen and just draw a big 1 where you entered the school building, if you know, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, here I don't see the area where we entered. I just know that through this auxiliary building we were taken out. This is where the truck was and this is where the wall was broken --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hold on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- this is the gym. This is the fence of the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you put a 1 next to the place where you were taken out where the wall was broken, where you've marked that red mark. Just put a 1 next to that so we know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a big mess, but this -- here where the mark is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's erase this one and try again. It's all right. We'll get it right. If you can, just put a 1 where you came out of the gym.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And -- that's good. And now let's save that, but can you just put the number 007 on this thing. Just put 007, that will indicate it's you, and just in the bottom right-hand corner, in the snow, put just 11/3/10, the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite the snow, but that will do. All right. Let's go to the next one and that is number 1128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you asking -- are you tendering this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was going to -- I have three of them. I was going to do it at the end if that would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Otherwise it's a danger to lose these markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence then and the -- and 1129 which -- it was the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I hear no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I think we had a discussion about the information sheet, the hard copy, that should be uploaded and we would receive that as well as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- yes, that's uploaded and we should offer that as well, 6188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet will be P42, under seal. And the photograph marked by the witness will be P43.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go now to 65 ter 1128.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you mark with a 2 if you recognise anything on this photograph -- do you -- first of all, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you make it brighter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's about as good as we get. And if you can't recognise it, don't worry about it; if you can, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance, and from here one went straight and then to the left and then there was a door leading straight into the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hold on. We've got another glitch. But just to try to make it as simple as you can, can you put a 2 where you came out of the gym, if you can see. Just put a 2 -- if you can see where you came out, just put a 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did put a 2 but it's not showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can see it, so it -- and that's just right. Can you tell on this photograph the area where you went into the school? If not, don't worry about it; if you can, put a 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. It's actually quite dark. I can't tell whether there's a door there or not. It's really dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have hard time seeing without my glasses and my glasses are really not the right prescription.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we're fine. If you can just in the right-hand corner put 007 again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That will work. And it's the same date, the 11 -- 11 March 2010.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, but let me ask, is it really necessary to have the date and the pseudonym on the photo? I don't think that this is really necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart always has told me to do that, Your Honour, but if -- that's just our practice and it's whatever you wish, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
