utterances.text: Not to do that could simplify the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, I'll try to see if I can remember why we do that. I'm sure there's a reason for it, but we'll sort it out. I've got only two more, so we're almost finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. We wait for the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be P44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to 65 ter 1134.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need you to mark anything on this right away, but do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are the doors through which we came in. This basketball hoop that's there now, I didn't see it back then; but otherwise it's the gym as it was. These are the windows and then the entire wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to point anything out to Mr. Ruez when you were there, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you point out to him, if you recall? You don't need to mark the photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed everything to him as it was. I came there and nothing had been done to the gym. There was some cupboards there that didn't used to be when we were kept there. So everything was -- looked normal. There was something that was built up, but yes, everything was normal as it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that, 1134, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go to one last exhibit, it is number 5755, page 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Witness, for your purposes, as you'll see, this is a list of names, and I will ask you if you recognise any of the names on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if you can read that. If we can blow it up a bit -- read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here is my brother. This is my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast, by the way. I apologise. And if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One second, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, this is the end of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. Now the accused has the chance in cross-examination to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am ready to start my cross-examination based on the statement provided by this witness. I would like to greet the witness, and this is how I am going to address him, and I would like to say that with all due respect for everything that he had gone through we nevertheless have to ask certain questions in order to clarify the situation that he has been describing because this situation and certain aspects can be perceived in a variety of different ways. On my behalf, I would like to express my condolences for all those who went through this ordeal. If I may begin with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness told us here that later, after he had reached the free territory, he learned from his brother that his brother passed him by in the bus column that was moving from Sandici to Potocari. I would like to ask him just to tell us a little bit more about this. How is what was possible for his brother to see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, my brother didn't see me. We were not moving from Sandici to Potocari, but rather to Bratunac. He only saw people who were captured, but he didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a bus. My brother who managed to cross over, he was a disabled person. He had -- he has sciatica and he was a disabled person. He was not a military disabled person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So he is talking about his brother who left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you here. You are both speaking the same language. You should avoid overlapping in asking and answering and -- for the sake of the interpretation. Just wait for the moment the transcript stops. Now put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What I would like to know was whether his brother at the time was in the bus along with those who were crossing from the Serbian territory to the Muslim territory or was he in some other means of transportation. That was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother was in Potocari. He had two crutches. That's how he walked. While he was in Potocari a Serbian soldier told him, "Get on the truck." And he said, "I can't do that." And then another one told him, "Well, then, go and board a bus," and that's what he did. Luckily, he managed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone. Mr. Tolimir, you need your microphone. Your microphone, you should switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, do you know anything about the agreement that was reached at Fontana between representatives of Srebrenica and representatives of the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They did not negotiate while we were in Srebrenica. If they did negotiate, that took place only after the people had left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe you didn't understand me properly. We are talking here about the fact that people were not allowed to leave Srebrenica before this agreement was informed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you know that Mladic was negotiating at Fontana, in Bratunac, with someone called Mandzic, I don't know. But we all had already left except women and children. You held them as hostages because if anything happened on the road you threatened to strangle all the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have to ask you as well to stop and to wait between -- not to answer immediately but to wait a little moment so that the transcript and the interpreters can follow what you are answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to add, it's not because I'm listening to the French, but I have the feeling that the witness is talking to the accused and the witness should actually be talking and looking at the Trial Chamber and not at the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would really like to clarify this situation which will enable me to ask the following question. So can the answer -- can the witness answer me whether in this column that was headed towards Tuzla knew that there had been an agreement according to which those fit for military services were supposed to surrender themselves as prisoners of war, whereas the civilian population was to be -- was to be transferred to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer because there were overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness didn't start with his answer. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe it will help, but the last part would have been not that the population was to be transferred to Srebrenica, but that the population was to be transferred out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you should please repeat your answer to the last question, especially related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people had left Srebrenica on the 11th of July. They went to Potocari, which is 4 kilometres from Srebrenica. So they were moving out of Srebrenica and heading towards the liberated territory or the free territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Obviously I cannot elicit an answer from the witness whether the Muslim people and the army knew that an agreement had been reached at Fontana. This is all I'm interested in because this is very important for my next questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, nobody told us anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since nobody told you anything about this agreement, then you didn't know that you were in violation of this agreement because you didn't surrender and you embarked on a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we did surrender. Didn't you see us? Didn't you see how we surrendered. Of the 1.000, only five or ten people managed to survive. That was a divine intervention that these people were saved. What are you trying to persuade us? We did surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just -- you should put questions to the witness and not make statements, and the last question was not a question, in fact. Keep that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked him whether the soldiers and the population of Srebrenica were aware about the Fontana agreement. I'm not trying to make any assessments and judgements about documents. I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you must not explain anything. Just ask questions. You must not explain why you are asking a question. Just put questions to the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to ask you, Mr. President, what you told me just now, to say the same thing to the witness. He is giving his own assessments, such as genocide and things. It's not up to him to use this kind of terminology. It is up to you to decide what terms are going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a question the Chamber has to deal with. In this respect we don't need your guidance. Please carry on asking questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is: Did you personally know, as well as those who were with you in the column, that an agreement had been reached at Fontana between representatives of the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, don't ask me that. You ask someone else about this. If I had known about this, I -- why should I have been such a foolish person and risk losing my life? Don't say things that are inappropriate to say. What are you talking about? What are you talking about Fontana for? That was already a time when people were dead, while Mladic and the rest of them were drinking whiskey at Fontana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you should just answer the question. We don't want to have debates on different positions. If the accused puts questions to you, just answer; if you don't know that, then say "I don't know." If you know, then tell the Chamber what you are -- what is your knowledge. I'm very sorry. Mr. Tolimir may ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your written statement and here in this courtroom today, you said that in the evening a certain man came to see us and somebody told you that that was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know him before that, but when I reached the free territory and when I saw him on TV that was 100 per cent Mladic. And he addressed us by saying, "Good evening, neighbours." Nobody else called us neighbours except him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you recall anything else that Mladic told you, apart from this word "neighbours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came he said, "Good evening, neighbours," and then he said, "The governments are in negotiations and there will be an exchange tomorrow, all for all." He also said, "You will get some water but no supper." In my view, what he meant was that there will be blood. He never mentioned food. Others mentioned food, but he thought that we would have blood; but bread, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You have answered my question, but I would like to ask you to give me a yes or no answer and let us give a chance to the Trial Chamber to make their own conclusions. My next question is -- today you said that this young man decided who to shoot and who -- whom he should not shoot. When this man said, "You mustn't kill all these people," my question is: Do you believe that this was also done according to his personal wish or according to someone's orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was ordered to do that or whether he himself wanted to do that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question. You also said that a young man with a black scarf let some children under the age of 15 and some women from the column of the prisoners. Was that his own decision? Did he do that on his own initiative or did he follow orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably at his own initiative. I don't think there was any of his superiors present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: Did you have the impression that many of those individuals who imprisoned you, treated you and decided on your life on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. While we were in the school building they never physically abused us. When other people came, probably officers dressed in camouflage uniforms, that's when orders were issued to take people out to be shot. So this was not done on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said from the moment when the people in camouflage uniforms came and those who asked you, "Is there anyone here from Zvornik," are you referring to those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we need the second technical break now. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber wants to come back to the last document, the list of names we saw on the screen. Perhaps it was not very clear the position the Chamber took, and especially after having heard the objection of Mr. Tolimir. The Chamber will receive this one page with the markings of this witness as an exhibit in evidence. And the Prosecution should come back to the other part of this whole document, this book, at a later stage when it seems to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Tolimir, once again, please pause between the answer and your next question and just recall that you should put questions to the witness. But I would like to say a word to the witness as well. The accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to put questions to you and you should -- and it is a very strange situation for you, I can imagine, but you should just listen to the question and answer this question. That would help the Chamber to find out the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could you please just advise me how much time I have at my disposal. Can I use the remainder of the day today for my question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course it's up to you how many questions do you have and we have time until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you said here during your testimony that on the sixth day you arrived in Baljkovica village, that was on page 43, lines 44 -- 24 and 25 in the transcript, to the place where the breakthrough occurred. However, you failed to mention on what day it was that you were re-captured after Baljkovica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't captured after Baljkovica. I was not taken prisoner. I was taken prisoner at Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you may provide a more precise answer. Before you were taken to Batkovici, were you captured? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I never was in Batkovici. Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me then about the breakthrough. You came to Baljkovica. Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the breakthrough was carried out, I went towards a village. I can't recall the name. I went in the direction of Nezuk village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you in the part of the column, the front part of the column that had broken through the line held by the Serb forces in the direction of Tuzla or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't with that column. I arrived after the column had already gone by. The column probably broke through around 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, and I arrived there in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer the next question, please pause. It is necessary for the sake of the interpretation, otherwise your answer will not be heard. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, at the end of your evidence here today you said that the president of the municipality was at the head of the column that was advancing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. I said that the leadership of the municipality was there, but I didn't say anything about him being either at the beginning or middle of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then answer this: This leadership, municipal leadership that was at the head of the column together with the armed group that advanced before a part of the column actually hit an ambush where 50 people were killed, was that column moving from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. They headed from Susnjari, and I don't know when exactly it was when they set off, whether it was at midnight or before midnight. All I know is that I set off on the next day, on the 12th, with the last group. So we set off from Susnjari, the last group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the room where you were held, where you first had to leave your equipment, and when you were asked by my learned colleague how many people were outside the school you said about 150 to 200. And then you said that once you entered the hall, you sat with your backs to one another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that there were lockers for about 200 people. I don't know how many. Because they only took off their coats and jackets. A person did not take all their clothes off. And as for those who arrived, when it was ordered that they should be blindfolded, they commanded that people who were up -- halfway in the hall, they should turn one way and the people on the other half of the hall should turn their -- towards the other wall in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me please whether -- I just want to check if I understood you correctly. You said that the hall was 15 by 20 metres long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say how large it was. It was a gym and it was measured at that point, but I don't know how -- what the measurements were. It was probably 12 metres wide to 15 -- by 15 to 16 metres long, but I don't recall it ever being actually written down how large it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. So you say that it was 12 to 15 metres long. You're not sure. But can you tell me now, is it possible to fit 1.000 people in that space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, the way we were crammed in, I think it is possible. Because, you see, my -- as I was sitting, my knees were actually up to my chin. They were against my breast, and I could -- if I was able to count, I could count up to ten men, you know, along one row and -- the length of the row and then also the width of the column. But there were a lot of vehicles, and if each vehicle had 50 people at least on it, and there were probably also people who were standing in the vehicles, then you can see how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago during your evidence you said that there were about 500 to 1.000 people there. Could you please tell us more specifically which of the two it is. I accept that you say -- if you say 1 to 2, that's okay; but if you say 500 to 1.000, that's quite a big difference. Now, could you tell us again, was it 500 people or 1.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. That was my estimate. But judging by how long it took for those people to be killed, it took some seven to eight hours, now you can take -- you can make the calculation yourself. If there was at least 30 people on a truck at least -- per truck because there could be ten people per bench, so judging by the vehicles and the number of people that got on them -- and then also there were people who were there from before, this is my rough estimate. Now, whether it was 700 or 800 people, I can't really say with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Prosecution on the 13th and 14th of August, 1995, under number 0079-8668, on page 2 you say: "No one organised the evacuation of able-bodied men. According to our then estimates there were around 15.000 men who were going through the woods." My question is this: Is it possible that no one organised the evacuation of a column numbering 15.000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not. These people started -- they set off on their own will, and even when it was -- when we heard that Srebrenica had fallen we were going towards Susnjari and women and children were going towards Potocari. How many people came from Suceska, I don't know. But if you weren't there to see the huge number of people who were gathered there, I don't really know. Maybe there were over 15.000 people or maybe not, but this is a very rough estimate. Because, you see, when we showed up there, we would fill two or three fields right away. And then when they started putting these people in files and columns, then it was very difficult to judge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last portion of your answer. Could you perhaps repeat the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said, there were some 15.000 people there because if you consider how many people there were there and that we couldn't set off right away, we only left at around 1.00, it was still day-time, and it is even possible that there were more people than that. But most probably there were around 15.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of July 1995, a few moments ago I mentioned your August 1995 statement, but in your July witness -- in your July statement, number 008483, you said the following: "Able-bodied men were organised in order -- organised themselves in order to leave Srebrenica" -- just a moment, please. Just wait for me to finish my question. Can you tell me, please, are these -- do these statements differ because one was given in July and one in August, or is it about something else? Where is this discrepancy arising from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause. Please pause. We are still waiting for interpretation. And now please start with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that able-bodied men fit for military service organised themselves, because people had problems. They had families, and as for me, I was over 40 even then, I wasn't young. And as I said, I wasn't even capable. After being in Srebrenica, I was so exhausted and I wondered whether I would be able to reach Tuzla at all. Because if I were to show you a document which showed -- with a picture after I arrived from Srebrenica, you couldn't believe what I looked like. I looked like a skeleton with just skin over it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. My assistant suggested that I repeat the ERN number of the July statement. The ERN number that I asked to be posted, because it has not been recorded in the transcript, that's number 0033-8483.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Could we ask -- I think it should be known that if there's going to be repeated references to previous statements, we will need to know the page and line in the English as well as the Serbian so that we can make reference to it. I haven't said anything at -- to this point, but if that could be borne in mind in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you made a point. Even the Chamber has no possibility to follow that way because we don't have these statements. Perhaps it is possible to make a clear reference to the page numbers in both languages, then we could perhaps, if you want to do that, call them up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. McCloskey. Could he please take a look at 1D002, it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I think we have a problem. We have to go to private session if that is displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will manage not to broadcast it to the public, only to have it on the screen in the courtroom, then this is possible. We must not go into private session. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is English version page 2, line 3. However, if this requires us to go into private session, I will not put any questions concerning this. I will skip over all of these questions. All I want is to ask this witness about how these statements were written up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, who wrote the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you type it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sign the version in the language that you understand or did you sign the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I signed the English version, but it was interpreted to me into my language. But perhaps what you're referring to is my statement from Tuzla. But I don't remember whether I signed it in Tuzla or not. I know that I signed the one that was in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the document 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, the document on the screen was a statement to the high court judge of Tuzla. He was speaking about the document to the Prosecutor. The witness clarified it is why I sat down, but -- so hopefully we can stay clear on which -- there's many, many statements over 15 years and we need to be very clear which statement we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was referring to 1D001, but if it's a problem I will not insist on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, if I signed it, it is my statement. I'm not going to disown it. It's just that it's been 15 years and I simply don't remember. I remember that it was in English and they interpreted it for me, and maybe there was a problem with interpretation. That's the only problem that could have been because I would never say anything against somebody. I try very, very hard not to do that. I read the solemn declaration that I would speak the truth, and I tried to do that as a witness. And I try not to raise my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I also want to ask you about your statement 0798668 [as interpreted], page 2, paragraph 6. Could we have it on the screen, please. You say there: "I was in a group where there were 100 men. Most of them were civilians. There were a couple of soldiers and several wounded men."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you here. We don't have it on the screen. Just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do we have the 65 ter number of the document so that it can be found?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Please look at 1D001, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it appears on the screen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is: Does it stem from your statements that the column was established by civilians who were able-bodied and that there were some soldiers in there? You said that there were about 500 rifles there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said about 500 rifles, but perhaps some of those people remained in the last column. However, they left the column immediately and went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did the mayor that you mentioned a bit earlier have any role in the column? You said that he was at the head of the column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him in the column at all, but I suppose that the leadership left within the first groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it's not a problem to say that in public session, did you have less than 50 years when you set out from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was younger than 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you fall in the category of able-bodied men, fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, based on my age, yes, but I was not a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you know that there is a category of those who are able-bodied, fit for military service and for work, you know what age that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from 18 until 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Isn't it that 15-year-old children are already considered fit for work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Tell me which law specifies that, that the age limit for that is 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's not necessary for us to debate on this. I just said that 15-year-olds are considered fit for work and people of age are 18-year-olds, but we don't need to discuss this. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since you went out in the field with Jean-Rene Ruez, did he give you any suggestions when the statement was taken and drafted, the statement that he co-signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you answer this, please: Were your families together with you and your brothers in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your proper attitude. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to thank you that you again were in the position to come to The Hague to testify here and to help the Chamber find out the truth. Thank you very much again, and you are now free to return to your home. Thank you very much and the Court Officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need to go into private session. I think so. Now everything is prepared. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have been told he has been sent back to his hotel. He's a rather elderly man and he is not here, but he'll of course be ready to go tomorrow. He, as you may recall, is a 92 ter witness so he will be very short for the Prosecution. And I wanted to mention to you, should he finish early, we have not brought any more witnesses in because of the long week it would have taken. But we do have an exhibit that we call the trial video, which the Defence has -- is fully aware of. And it's basically the videos that have been put together from films shot by combat cameras and journalists, beginning with 10 July in -- and the military movement towards Srebrenica, through Srebrenica, into Potocari, the Hotel Fontana meetings you heard briefly about. And we had normally played that with Mr. Ruez so that if questions pop up he could answer them, though he -- in the past there haven't been too many questions. I was thinking we might be able to save some time, if we have at least an hour or so extra, we could play portions of that video for you to -- and that way we would have less time to take up with Mr. Ruez, who should be here in a couple of weeks. And hopefully we'll be able to get Mr. Ruez done in the three days that we have allotted for him. And so I've mentioned that to the Defence. Of course I offer that to you as well. This is a rather important video to see. We usually play it all in one chunk, but it's in day-oriented chapters, and it's something that I think we can -- it would be helpful for the Chamber to see if we can see it for an hour or so at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's in the moment, your decision what you want to present. We will, of course, consider that, but just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you want to make a comment to this request of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with this video footage. I don't know who shot that video footage and I don't know whether it can affect the opinion of the Trial Chamber or whether it has some other purpose as a document. That's all I can say right now. Perhaps later on I could be more specific later on, and if this document is so important for Mr. Ruez, then perhaps it needs to be shown when Mr. Ruez is here rather than tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have a bit of a problem. I have informed Mr. Gajic of this video - I'm sure he's very familiar with it - to get the word to the General. And if that communication is not going to work, I'm going to need to be able to try to communicate directly with the General and have some form to do that because this is going to be a long trial. It's going to be even longer if this basic daily communication to help alleviate the court schedule is not done. Perhaps they'd just forgotten or hadn't had a chance to talk, but I sincerely hope that this is not the way we have to communicate with the General in open court because we'll end up spending a lot of time talking between lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you want to say something, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Mr. Gajic told me that Mr. McCloskey wanted to show a video footage from the Popovic et al. case. However, he had indicated that he was going to change something in this video footage, therefore that's why I said that I'm not familiar with the contents. My legal advisor just told me that Mr. McCloskey had advised him that he was going to make some changes in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is video that the Defence has had for months and months, and the -- there are -- there are no -- there's nothing new about any of this video. The actual piece that was played in Popovic will have a couple of additional pieces added to it later on down the road, but the first hour and -- roughly hour, hour and a half is identical to what was played in the Popovic. And then there will be little additions of video that they've had for months, like I say. So there's no real -- there's no changes, so to speak, and there's certainly nothing new in the first hour and a half. This is the famous footage that's been on television all over the world for years and years. There's no mystery to this. It's General Mladic, his troops, Potocari. They know what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary to continue this debate today. We will see what will happen tomorrow in the courtroom when this witness arrives, and we will deal with that later. I would like to raise the problem of protective measures for the next witness. The Prosecution moved to give this -- these protective measures as in the last trial. The Defence objected. The position of the Chamber is the same as with the last witness. I think it is not necessary repeat all arguments. Pursuant to our Rules, Rule 75 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we are bound by the decision of the last -- the previous Chamber and there is no argument put to the Chamber to vary or to rescind anything of these protective measures. And in that way, like with the last witness, the application of the Prosecution is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have actually filed, as you see, official motion notifications requests on these two witnesses, but as we agree with the Trial Chamber, this is a matter of law already decided. Would you prefer us to continue to file formal motions with the Registry in these situations where things are identical to what they were before, or we can also just merely inform the parties that we are standing by on the protective measures that were there before and only file if there's a change. But we can do it either way. It's just whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is always in favour of the most -- of the way to deal with these problems in the most simple way, and therefore if there is no objection by the Defence, it should be just a notification that everybody is aware of the protective measures granted by previous Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be the simplest way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think at this stage we adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
